title: Stretching and springs: what pulls a band back?

summary.text: A stretched rubber band snaps back when you let go, but nothing pushed it, so what pulled it? The child hangs coins on a band, 5 at a time, and finds the pattern with their own hands. Each equal handful adds about the same stretch, until a spring is pulled too far and stays long. Deep down, a solid's shape is where the pulls between its atoms balance. A pull too far lets atoms settle beside new neighbours. The same springiness works in tendons, spider webs and the rocks that bend for centuries before an earthquake.
summary.art: A child hanging a paper cup of coins from a rubber band beside a ruler; behind, faint pictures of a pen spring, an ankle tendon, a spider web and bent layers of rock under mountains.

intro.hook: Hold a rubber band between two fingers and stretch it a little. Feel it pull on your fingers. Stretch it more. Does the pull get bigger? Nothing is pushing the band. So where does the pull come from?
intro.text: Give your child a rubber band and let them stretch it slowly, then let it go back. Ask two questions. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Good noticing sounds like 'the more I stretch it, the harder it pulls' or 'it gets thinner'. Write their wonders down and don't answer them yet. The coin test comes next, and it lets them find the answers for themselves.
intro.art: A child's two fingers stretching a rubber band, with small arrows showing the band pulling back on each finger, and a question mark in the middle of the band.

outcomes: I can say what elastic means: a thing changes shape when pushed or pulled, and goes back when you let go. I can name elastic things at home.
I can guess, with a reason, what equal handfuls of coins will do to a rubber band. Then I can test it fairly and find the pattern.
I can explain the elastic limit: pull too far and a thing stays stretched or snaps. I can find where a pen spring stops coming back.
I can explain that a stretched or squashed spring stores energy, and give uses like catapults, wind-up toys, bows and bouncing balls.
I can find springs in machines, in nature and in my own body, and say what job each one does.
I can explain, deep down, why things spring back: each atom rests where the pulls from its neighbours balance. Past the limit, atoms settle beside new neighbours, so the shape changes for good.

I can give big examples of stretching: rock storing strain before an earthquake, the Earth ringing like a bell, and space itself stretching as gravitational waves pass. I can say what scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces can make things move, stop, turn or change shape.
terms.example: You pull a rubber band. You squash a sponge. Both are forces.
terms.art: Two hands: one pulling a rubber band, one squashing a sponge.

terms.meaning: To pull something so it gets longer.
terms.example: You stretch a rubber band round a bundle of pencils.
terms.art: A rubber band before and after stretching, with a ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: To push on something so it gets shorter or flatter. Scientists also say compress.
terms.example: Pressing the top of a clicky pen squashes the spring inside.
terms.art: A spring being squashed flat by a thumb.

terms.meaning: A thing is elastic if it changes shape when pushed or pulled, and goes back to its old shape when you let go.
terms.example: A rubber band, a spring, a sponge and a bouncy ball are all elastic.
terms.art: Four things in a row, each shown squashed or stretched, then back to normal.

terms.meaning: A coil of springy metal wire. Pull it and it gets longer. Squash it and it gets shorter. Let go and it goes back.
terms.example: There is a small spring inside a clicky ballpoint pen.
terms.art: A clicky pen opened up, with its little spring lying beside it.

terms.meaning: To go back to the old shape after being stretched, squashed or bent.
terms.example: Press a sponge. Let go. It springs back.
terms.art: A sponge, pressed and then puffed back up.

terms.meaning: A thing that changes shape and stays changed when you let go. Scientists call this plastic, which is a different meaning from plastic bags.
terms.example: Playdough, chewing gum and a strip from a thin carry bag stay stretched.
terms.art: A ball of playdough pulled long, staying long after the hands let go.

terms.meaning: A thing that hardly bends at all, then suddenly breaks. Scientists call this brittle.
terms.example: A dry twig, a papad and a glass bangle snap.
terms.art: A dry twig snapping in two, with a little crack line.

terms.meaning: The furthest you can stretch a thing and still have it spring back. Go past it and the thing stays stretched or breaks.
terms.example: Pull a pen spring very hard. It stays long and wobbly. It went past its elastic limit.
terms.art: Two pen springs: one neat, one pulled long and loose.

terms.meaning: The rule that, for small stretches, equal extra pulls give equal extra stretches. Robert Hooke wrote it down in 1678.
terms.example: In the coin test, each 5 coins made the band longer by about the same step.
terms.art: A spring hanging beside a ruler with one, two and three equal weights, its length growing by equal steps.

terms.meaning: How much a thing has been stretched, squashed or bent, compared with its own size. A bent thing holds its strain until it springs back.
terms.example: Rock deep under the Himalaya is slowly bent by moving land. It is storing strain.
terms.art: A long block of rock bent gently like a pressed ruler, with small arrows showing the squeeze.

terms.meaning: The force a stretched or squashed thing makes as it tries to go back to its old shape. Scientists call it the restoring force.
terms.example: A stretched rubber band pulls back on your fingers.
terms.art: Two fingers holding a stretched band, with small arrows pointing inwards.

terms.meaning: Hard to stretch or bend. A stiff spring needs a big pull to stretch a little.
terms.example: A cycle seat spring is much stiffer than a pen spring.
terms.art: A thick cycle seat spring next to a thin pen spring.

terms.meaning: Energy waiting inside something, ready to be used. A stretched or squashed spring stores energy.
terms.example: When you let go of a stretched catapult, the stored energy flings the paper ball.
terms.art: A popsicle-stick catapult, bent back, with a glowing 'stored energy' halo.

terms.meaning: When a thing hits the ground, squashes a little, then springs back and jumps up.
terms.example: A rubber ball bounces high. A ball of clay just goes splat.
terms.art: A rubber ball squashed flat for a moment on the floor, then rising.

terms.meaning: A graph where dots are joined by a line. It shows how one thing changes as another thing changes.
terms.example: A line graph can show how long a rubber band gets as you add more coins.
terms.art: A simple line graph going up in a straight line.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Your rubber band is made of countless atoms, all holding on to each other.
terms.art: A zoom from a rubber band to a tangle of chains to tiny balls.

terms.meaning: The pull that holds two atoms together. A bond acts a bit like a tiny spring between them.
terms.example: Stretching a steel spring pulls each pair of atoms a tiny bit apart. The bond between them pulls them back together.
terms.art: Balls joined by small springs, like a ball-and-spring toy.

terms.meaning: A very long chain made of many small bits joined in a row. Rubber is made of polymers.
terms.example: Rubber is made of long, tangled chains, like a bowl of cooked noodles.
terms.art: A bowl of tangled noodles next to a drawing of tangled rubber chains.

terms.meaning: A strong, stretchy cord that joins a muscle to a bone. Tendons work like springs when you run and jump.
terms.example: The thick cord at the back of your ankle is your Achilles tendon.
terms.art: A child's leg with the Achilles tendon glowing at the back of the ankle.

terms.meaning: A sudden shaking of the ground. It happens when rocks that were slowly bent underground suddenly slip and spring back.
terms.example: The ground shakes, and the lights swing.
terms.art: Two blocks of rock bent like a ruler, then slipping with a jolt.

terms.meaning: A ripple in space itself. As it passes, it stretches space one way and squeezes it the other way, by an incredibly tiny amount.
terms.example: In 2015, scientists first caught a gravitational wave from two black holes that crashed together.
terms.art: A grid of space rippling out from two black holes spiralling together.

terms.meaning: To shake back and forth very fast. A plucked rubber band vibrates because it keeps springing back past its middle.
terms.example: Pluck a stretched rubber band. It blurs and hums.
terms.art: A plucked rubber band with blur lines and a little musical note.

explanations.definition: A thing is elastic if it changes shape when a force pushes or pulls it, and goes back to its old shape when the force stops.
explanations.description: Pull a rubber band and it gets longer. Let go and it snaps back. Squeeze a sponge and it gets smaller. Let go and it puffs back up. Both are elastic. Being elastic is not only about stretching. Things can also be squashed, bent or twisted and then spring back. Here is a surprise. Steel, wood, stone and even glass are a little elastic too. They just need a much bigger force before you can see them change.
examples: A hair band stretches round your hair, then goes back to its small loop.
A plastic ruler bends when you press its end, then springs straight.
A cricket ball squashes a tiny bit when the bat hits it, then springs back round.
explanations.art: Four panels: a rubber band stretched and back, a sponge squeezed and back, a ruler bent and back, a ball squashed and back.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what it means for something to be elastic.

explanations.definition: For small stretches, equal extra pulls give equal extra stretches. Double the pull and you get about double the stretch. This rule is called Hooke's law.
explanations.description: In the coin test, each 5 coins made the band longer by about the same step. Why? Each 5 coins pull down by the same amount. The band stretches until its pull back matches the pull of the coins. Suppose the pull back grows by the same amount for each step of stretch. Then equal coins must give equal steps. Robert Hooke wrote this rule down in 1678. He put it in Latin: 'ut tensio, sic vis'. It means 'as the stretch, so the force'. Steel springs follow it closely, for small stretches. Rubber bands follow it only roughly. Their steps often grow a little as the band gets long. This rule is why a spring balance has evenly spaced marks. The unit on measuring forces looks at spring balances more closely.
examples: One bag of shopping stretches the spring of a luggage scale a little. Two bags stretch it about twice as far.
A thick rubber band needs a bigger pull than a thin one to stretch the same amount. Scientists say it is stiffer.
explanations.art: A rubber band hanging from a pencil with a paper cup below it, coins going in, and a ruler beside it.
explanations.context: Remember the coin test, where you added 5 coins at a time and measured the band? This card explains the pattern you found.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

explanations.concept: The elastic limit: spring back, stay stretched, or snap
explanations.definition: Every elastic thing has a limit. Stretch it less than its limit and it springs back. Stretch it past its limit and it stays stretched, or it snaps.
explanations.description: Pull a pen spring gently and it springs back neatly. Pull it hard and it stays long and loose. It has gone past its elastic limit. Scientists sort materials into three kinds. Elastic things spring back, like rubber. Stay-changed things, like playdough and chewing gum, keep their new shape. Scientists call this plastic. Snapping things, like a dry twig or a papad, hardly bend before they break. Scientists call this brittle. Many things do all three. A steel spoon springs back from a small bend. Push hard and it stays bent. Bend it back and forth many times and it can snap.
examples: Bend a steel hairpin a little and it springs back. Bend it hard and it stays bent.
A green twig bends and springs back. A dry twig snaps.
A strip cut from a thin carry bag stretches long and stays long.
explanations.art: Three hands: one pulling a rubber band that springs back, one pulling playdough that stays long, one bending a dry twig that snaps.
explanations.context: Remember the pen spring that came back from small pulls but stayed long after a big one? This card explains what happened.

explanations.concept: Deep down: a shape is a balance of pulls
explanations.definition: A solid keeps its shape because each atom rests where the pulls and pushes from its neighbours balance. Stretch a little and those pulls bring the atoms back. Stretch too far and rows of atoms slip, and each atom settles beside new neighbours.
explanations.description: Zoom far into a steel spring. You find atoms in neat rows. Each atom is held to its neighbours by electric pulls called bonds. Push two atoms too close and they push apart. Pull them a little apart and they pull together. So each atom rests at the one place where the push and the pull balance. Stretching the spring moves every atom a tiny bit from that place. The further it moves, the harder the bonds pull it back. That is why equal coins gave equal steps. Now pull much too far. Whole rows of atoms slip past each other, like cards sliding in a pack. Each atom now holds on to new neighbours, and rests in a new balance. Let go, and nothing pulls it back to the old place. That is why the pen spring stayed long. Its atoms are the same atoms. Only which atoms hold which has changed. Atoms on their bonds are never perfectly still. They jiggle all the time, even at the coldest temperature possible.
examples: Scientists often build models of solids with little balls joined by springs.
Bend a steel spoon a little and it springs back. Bend it hard and it stays bent, because rows of its atoms have slipped.
Heat makes atoms jiggle more on their bonds. That is why a metal rod gets very slightly longer when it is hot.

Some wire, called memory metal, goes back to its old shape when you warm it. Its atoms have two ways of sitting in rows. Warmth moves them back to the first way. Scientists call this shape memory. How a metal can keep a shape and return to it is still a wonder to think about.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a pen spring; the wire; rows of atoms held by small arrows that balance; one row slipped along, each atom beside new neighbours.
explanations.context: This card zooms in far past anything a microscope can show. It explains why things spring back, and why a big pull changes them for good.

explanations.concept: A long band is many springs in a row
explanations.definition: A long spring stretches more than a short one, because it is like many short springs joined in a row. A thick band stretches less, because it is like many thin bands side by side, sharing the pull.
explanations.description: In the Two in a Row activity, two bands in a chain stretched about twice as far as one band. Each band in the chain carries the whole weight of the coins. So each stretches as much as one band alone. Side by side, each band carries only half the weight, so the pair stretches about half as far. Atoms work the same way. A long wire has more bonds in a row. Each bond stretches a tiny bit, and all the tiny bits add up. Robert Hooke used this idea. A short wire hardly seemed to stretch at all. So he hung weights from a wire 20 to 40 feet long, about 6 to 12 metres. Then the stretch became big enough to measure.
examples: A long rubber band stretches further than a short one of the same thickness, with the same coins.
A bungee cord is many thin rubber strands side by side, so it can hold a person.
A thick rope stretches less than a thin string, because it has more fibres sharing the pull.
explanations.art: Two rubber bands hooked in a chain holding a cup of coins, beside two bands side by side holding the same cup, with rulers showing the chain twice as long.
explanations.context: Why does a long band stretch more than a short one, and a thick band less? This card explains, from coins down to atoms.

explanations.definition: Rubber is made of very long, tangled chains of atoms called polymers. Stretching straightens the chains. They spring back because jiggling atoms shake them back into a tangle.
explanations.description: Think of a bowl of cooked noodles, all tangled. Pull them and they line up straight. In rubber, the chains are joined to each other here and there, so they cannot slide apart. When you let go, the chains are shaken by the jiggling of heat. Tangled is far more likely than straight, so they wriggle back into a tangle. This is why rubber does odd things. It warms up a little when you stretch it fast. A stretched rubber band even pulls harder when you heat it. Stretch rubber very far, again and again, and some of the links between chains slip or break. That is why an old, over-used band is longer and looser than a new one.
examples: A rubber band left round a newspaper for months goes long and floppy.
Cold rubber goes stiff, because its chains jiggle less.
explanations.art: A bowl of tangled noodles, then the same noodles pulled straight, then rubber chains tangled and straightened beside them.
explanations.context: A steel spring and a rubber band both spring back, but for different reasons. This card explains rubber's secret.

explanations.concept: Springs: stretch springs and squash springs
explanations.definition: A spring is a coil of springy metal wire. Some springs are made to be stretched, and some are made to be squashed. Both push or pull back when you let go.
explanations.description: A stretch spring has its coils packed tightly together. You pull its ends apart. A squash spring has gaps between its coils. You press its ends together. The spring in a clicky pen is a squash spring. The spring inside a spring balance at the vegetable shop is a stretch spring. Making the wire into a coil lets a short piece of stiff steel stretch a long way. Each bit of the wire twists only a little, but all the little twists add up.
examples: A clicky pen has a squash spring. It pushes the tip back in.
A trampoline has stretch springs all round its edge.
A clothes peg has a twisty spring that snaps its jaws shut.
explanations.art: Two springs side by side: a stretch spring with tight coils being pulled, and a squash spring with gaps being pressed.
explanations.context: Springs are hiding in pens, beds and cycles. This card explains the two main kinds.

explanations.definition: When you stretch, squash, bend or twist an elastic thing, the work you do is stored inside it. Let go, and the stored energy can make something move.
explanations.description: Energy is what it takes to make something move, warm up or change. When you pull back a catapult, your arm puts energy into the stretched rubber. When you let go, the rubber springs back and gives that energy to the stone or paper ball. The more you stretch, the more energy is stored, until the elastic limit. People have used stored elastic energy for thousands of years. Bows fling arrows. Wind-up watches and toys run on a tightly coiled spring. Some old mechanical clocks run for a whole week on one winding.
examples: A wind-up toy car runs when its twisted spring unwinds.
A bow made of bamboo bends back, stores energy, and flings the arrow.
A twisted rubber band can turn the propeller of a toy plane.
explanations.art: A child pulling back a bamboo bow, with a glowing band showing energy stored in the bent bow.
explanations.context: Why does a stretched catapult fling a paper ball? This card explains that stretching stores energy.

explanations.concept: Bouncing is a squash and a spring back
explanations.definition: When a ball hits the floor, it squashes for a very short moment. Then it springs back and pushes itself up. That is a bounce.
explanations.description: The squash is too quick to see. Slow-motion films show a tennis ball going flat on one side when it lands. Wet a ball and drop it on a dry floor. The wet mark shows how big the squashed part was. No ball bounces all the way back up. Some of the energy turns into heat and sound each time. A rubber ball keeps more of its energy, so it bounces higher. A ball of clay is not elastic. It squashes and stays squashed, so it does not bounce at all. Tennis has a rule about bounce. A tennis ball dropped from 254 cm must bounce back up between 135 cm and 147 cm.
examples: A bouncy rubber ball bounces higher than a sponge ball.
A trampoline's springs and stretchy mat squash down under you, then push you up.
explanations.art: A slow-motion strip: a ball falling, squashing flat on the floor, then springing back up a little lower than it started.
explanations.context: Why do some balls bounce high and others don't bounce at all? This card explains what a bounce really is.

explanations.definition: Living bodies are full of elastic parts. Tendons, skin, lungs and blood vessels stretch and spring back. Some animals store energy in springs to jump.
explanations.description: When you run, the tendon at the back of your ankle stretches as you land. It springs back as you push off. Tests show that a tendon gives back about nine-tenths of the energy put into it. That saves your muscles work. The arch of your foot is a spring too. Kangaroos hop a long way on huge springy tendons in their legs. A flea jumps with a pad of a rubbery stuff called resilin. Torkel Weis-Fogh, a Danish scientist, discovered resilin in insects in 1960. The flea's muscles squash the pad slowly and lock it. Then it lets go all at once, far faster than any muscle could move. A spider's web catches a flying insect by stretching. The sticky spiral threads can stretch to more than twice their length, soak up the insect's speed, then pull back. Your skin springs back because of a stretchy stuff called elastin. Your biggest blood vessel stretches with each heartbeat and springs back. Inside your muscles is titin, the biggest protein your body makes. It works like a tiny spring.
examples: Pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. It springs back.
A spider's web sags when an insect hits it, instead of breaking, then springs back.
The mantis shrimp, a sea animal, punches with a spring in its arm. Sheila Patek and her team filmed it in 2004.
explanations.art: A child mid-jump with the Achilles tendon glowing; around them a kangaroo, a flea, a spider web and a mantis shrimp.
explanations.context: Your body is full of springs. This card looks at the elastic parts of living things, from tendons to flea legs.

explanations.concept: Bend, don't break: why springy things survive
explanations.definition: A thing that can bend and spring back can take a sudden heavy push without breaking. A stiff, brittle thing may snap instead.
explanations.description: When a heavy load suddenly lands on something, its energy has to go somewhere. A springy thing bends, stores the energy for a moment, then gives it back. A stiff, brittle thing cannot bend, so the force builds up until it cracks. That is why bamboo bends in a storm instead of snapping. A green mango branch bends under a swing and springs back. Bent past its limit, it stays bent, and that is the warning that it may break. Tall buildings are designed to sway a little in strong winds, for the same reason.
examples: A coconut palm bends far over in a cyclone and often stands up again.
A car's springs bend over a bump, so the car does not crack.
explanations.art: A tall bamboo bending in a strong wind beside a dry stick snapping.
explanations.context: Is it better to be stiff or to bend? This card explains why bending and springing back can be stronger than being stiff.

explanations.concept: The Earth is springy: earthquakes and a ringing planet
explanations.definition: Rock is elastic too. Where giant pieces of the Earth's crust press together, the rock bends slowly and stores strain. When it suddenly slips, it springs back, and the ground shakes. That is an earthquake.
explanations.description: The Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces called plates. They move slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. The plate India sits on is pushing north into Asia. Where two plates press together, the rock gets stuck. It bends slowly, like a ruler pressed at one end, and stores strain. Across the Himalaya, GPS stations show the rock being squeezed by about 2 centimetres a year. This can go on for hundreds of years. Then the rock slips and springs back in seconds, and the ground shakes. That happened in Nepal on 25 April 2015. Harry Fielding Reid, an American scientist, explained this in 1910. He studied the great San Francisco earthquake of 1906. Earthquake waves can travel through the Earth only because rock is springy. In 1960 there was a giant earthquake in Chile. Afterwards, instruments found the whole Earth vibrating slowly for days, like a struck bell.
examples: The Himalayas are still being pushed up, which is why north India and Nepal have earthquakes.
Bend a plastic ruler slowly until it slips off your finger. It springs back with a twang, like rock in an earthquake.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the ground with two blocks of rock bent like a pressed ruler, then springing back with shaking lines above.
explanations.context: Can the ground stretch and spring back like a rubber band? This card shows how the bending of rock causes earthquakes.

explanations.definition: Space can stretch and squeeze. When huge things like black holes crash together, they send out ripples in space called gravitational waves.
explanations.description: Albert Einstein predicted these ripples in 1916. As a wave passes, space stretches one way and squeezes the other way, then back again. On 14 September 2015, two giant instruments in the United States, called LIGO, caught one for the first time. It came from two black holes that crashed together more than a billion years ago. The wave stretched LIGO's 4-kilometre-long arms by less than a hundredth of the width of a proton. A proton is a speck inside an atom. More than a thousand scientists worked on it, including teams from India. India is now building its own detector, called LIGO-India, in Maharashtra. The whole universe is stretching too. Galaxies are slowly getting further apart, because the space between them is growing.
examples: Draw dots on a wide rubber band and stretch it. Every dot moves away from every other dot, a little like galaxies in our growing universe.
A gravitational wave passing through you would stretch you a tiny bit taller and thinner. Then it would make you shorter and wider.
explanations.art: Two black holes spiralling together, sending rings of stretched and squeezed space across a grid towards a tiny Earth.
explanations.context: Stretching is not only for rubber bands. This card is about space itself stretching and squeezing.

explanations.concept: What is space, that it can stretch?
explanations.description: We know space can stretch, squeeze and ripple. We have measured it. But what is space made of, that it can do this? Is it a kind of stuff, like the rubber of a rubber band? Or is stretching just a way of describing distances between things changing? Nobody knows for sure. This is one of the deepest open questions in physics.
examples: A rubber sheet with a heavy ball on it is often used to picture bent space. It is a helpful picture, but space is not really a rubber sheet.

perspectives.who: Einstein's theory of gravity, called general relativity
perspectives.explanation: Space and time together bend, stretch and ripple. The theory describes this very well. It does not say what space is made of.

perspectives.who: Some physicists working on string theory
perspectives.explanation: Everything might be made of incredibly tiny vibrating strings, a little like plucked rubber bands. Space itself might come from them. Nobody has found any evidence yet that this is true.

perspectives.who: Other physicists, working on ideas like loop quantum gravity
perspectives.explanation: Space might be made of tiny pieces, like the threads of a woven net, far too small to ever see. This idea also has no evidence yet.

explanations.art: A child holding a stretched rubber band up to a starry sky, with a question mark made of rippling grid lines.
explanations.context: Scientists have measured space stretching. This card asks a question nobody can yet answer: what is space, that it can stretch?

agreed.text: Elastic things change shape when pushed or pulled, and go back when the force stops.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test this with rubber bands, springs and sponges. Engineers test steel, wood and concrete the same way, with big machines that stretch and squash them.

agreed.text: For many springs, double the pull gives about double the stretch, up to a limit.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hooke tested springs and long wires and published the rule in 1678. In the coin test, each 5 coins add about the same stretch. Spring balances work because of it.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

agreed.text: Every elastic thing has a limit. Past it, the thing stays stretched or breaks.
agreed.evidence: Stretch a pen spring hard and it stays long. Engineers measure the limit of every material used in bridges and buildings.

agreed.text: A solid keeps its shape because of electric pulls and pushes between its atoms. Past the elastic limit, rows of atoms slip into new places.
agreed.evidence: X-rays show that the atoms in metals sit in neat rows. Electron microscopes show the slipped rows inside metal that was bent too far.

agreed.text: A stretched or squashed elastic thing stores energy, which it gives back when it springs back.
agreed.evidence: Catapults, bows, wind-up clocks and bouncing balls all use it. Scientists measure the energy that goes in and comes out.

agreed.text: Earthquakes happen when bent rock underground suddenly slips and springs back.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured how the ground had bent before and after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Today GPS stations measure rock slowly bending across the Himalaya.

challenging.claim: Stretchy things are weak, and strong things are stiff.
challenging.for: A rubber band breaks easily, while a steel rod does not stretch at all that we can see.
challenging.against: Spider silk is very stretchy and, weight for weight, stronger than steel wire. Living roots and bamboo survive storms because they bend. Being able to stretch can make a thing tougher, because it soaks up a sudden push instead of cracking.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only stiff things can be strong.

challenging.claim: Hooke's rule works for every springy thing, however far you stretch it.
challenging.who: Robert Hooke himself, in 1678, and many people since
challenging.for: Hooke found equal steps in metal springs, long wires and dry wood. Steel springs follow the rule very closely for small stretches.
challenging.against: Rubber bands follow it only roughly. Their steps often grow as the band gets long. And every spring breaks the rule once it is pulled past its elastic limit. Then the steps stop being equal, and the spring stays long. Hooke's rule is very useful, but it is a rule for small stretches.
challenging.context: Robert Hooke found a rule for how springs stretch. This card asks whether his rule always works.

challenging.claim: Robert Hooke alone discovered the rule for springs, and invented the spring for watches.
challenging.for: Hooke published the spring rule in 1678. He also worked on springs to control watches in the 1660s.
challenging.against: Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, built a watch with a spiral spring in 1675. The two men argued bitterly about who was first. Hooke had hidden his spring rule in a code of jumbled letters in 1676. That way nobody could steal it before he was ready. Historians still disagree about the watch spring. The spring rule is fairly given to Hooke. In France, Edme Mariotte found the same rule on his own a few years later.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering how springs work.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton had the only portrait of Robert Hooke destroyed.
challenging.who: A story often told about Hooke and Newton, who were rivals
challenging.for: No portrait of Hooke survives from his lifetime. Newton disliked Hooke, and he led the Royal Society, the science club where a portrait might have hung.
challenging.against: Nobody has found any evidence that Newton destroyed a portrait. It may simply have been lost. In the 2000s an artist, Rita Greer, painted new portraits of Hooke from written descriptions of him.
challenging.context: Robert Hooke found the rule for how springs stretch. This card is about a story of why we do not know what he looked like.

challenging.claim: Rubber was invented in Europe or America, by people like Charles Goodyear.
challenging.for: Charles Goodyear found in 1839 how to make rubber tough with heat and sulphur. That made car tyres and rubber bands possible.
challenging.against: About 3,500 years ago, people in Mexico and Central America were already making bouncy rubber balls. In 1999, Dorothy Hosler and her team at MIT showed how. They mixed the milky sap of the rubber tree with juice from a morning glory vine. Different mixtures made rubber that bounced more, or rubber that was tougher.
challenging.context: This card is about who first made rubber, the stuff of rubber bands and bouncy balls.

challenging.claim: Cold would not matter to the rubber seals on the space shuttle Challenger.
challenging.who: Managers at NASA and at the company that made the booster rockets, in January 1986
challenging.for: The seals had worked on earlier flights. The managers were under pressure to launch on time.
challenging.against: An engineer called Roger Boisjoly warned the night before that cold rubber goes stiff and springs back too slowly. The launch went ahead on a freezing morning. A seal failed, and the shuttle broke apart. The seven astronauts on board died. Later, the scientist Richard Feynman squeezed a piece of the seal rubber in a small clamp. He dipped it in iced water during the inquiry. When he let go, it stayed squashed for a few seconds instead of springing back.
challenging.context: This card is a sad true story. It shows why it matters how fast rubber springs back.

challenging.claim: A branch that is bending is about to break.
challenging.for: Branches do break when they are bent too far.
challenging.against: Bending by itself is safe. A green branch bends in every breeze and springs back. The warning sign is a branch that bends and does not come all the way back. That means it has passed its elastic limit. Engineers watch for this same sign in cranes and bridges.
challenging.context: This card is about how to tell when something that bends is in danger, and when it is fine.

big_questions.q: A rubber band always goes back to its shape. Some people say it remembers. Others say its particles just pull back together. What do you think, and why?
big_questions.hint: Think of each atom resting where the pulls from its neighbours balance.

big_questions.q: Why should equal handfuls of coins give equal steps of stretch? What would have to be true inside the band?
big_questions.hint: Think of each bond as a tiny spring. What if each tiny spring pulls back a little harder for each bit it is stretched?

big_questions.q: Is anything completely stiff? Does a brick stretch even a tiny bit when you stand on it?
big_questions.hint: Hooke saw a long wire stretch when a short one seemed not to. How could you show a brick bending?

big_questions.q: When you stretch a catapult, where is the energy while you are holding it? Where does it go after you let go?
big_questions.hint: Think of the atoms pulled out of their resting places, and then the flying paper ball.

big_questions.q: After a big pull, the pen spring rests at a new length, and springs back to that. Is it the same spring as before?
big_questions.hint: All its atoms are still there. What has changed is which atoms hold which.

big_questions.q: Rock under the Himalaya is being bent a little every year, and nobody can see it. How can anyone know that something is storing strain before it breaks?
big_questions.hint: Think of the swing branch that stopped coming all the way back. What do GPS stations measure?

big_questions.q: A flea, a kangaroo and you all use springs to move. Why might living things have ended up so full of springs?
big_questions.hint: A spring gives back most of the energy you put in. Why would that help an animal that runs or jumps every day?

big_questions.q: Space itself stretches. What could space be made of, that it can stretch?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. What would you guess, and how could anyone ever test it?

big_questions.q: People in Mexico made bouncy rubber 3,500 years ago, but the books often credit someone else. Why do some inventors get remembered and others get forgotten?
big_questions.hint: Who wrote the books? Who was allowed to write?

big_questions.q: An engineer warned that cold rubber would not spring back fast enough, and the launch went ahead. How should people decide when a test result means 'stop'?
big_questions.hint: Feynman showed it with a glass of iced water. What made his test so hard to argue with?

story.title: The Tired Branch
story.note: Rubber tapping in Kerala, smoked rubber sheets and the Onam swing, the oonjal, are real. Ammu, her family, Biju and the mango tree are made up. The warning sign in the story is real physics: a branch or spring that no longer springs all the way back has gone past its elastic limit, and may soon break.
text: In a village near Kottayam, in Kerala, the rubber trees stand in long straight rows, like children lined up for school. Every morning before the sun was up, Ammu's mother walked between them with a lamp on her forehead and a curved knife in her hand. On each tree she shaved a thin spiral strip of bark. Out of the cut crept a white, slow milk, which ran down the spiral into a coconut-shell cup. Latex, her mother called it. Rubber before it knows it is rubber.

Ammu was ten. Her job came after school. She carried the full cups home, poured the latex into flat trays and helped her mother squeeze it into sheets through the iron rollers in the shed. Then the sheets were hung in the smoke above the fire to dry, brown and shining, like enormous dosas.

Before any sheet was sold, her mother tested it. She took one corner between her finger and thumb and pulled. A good sheet stretched, and then, when she let go, slid back flat as if nothing had happened. Once Ammu found an old sheet that had been forgotten in the sun for weeks. When her mother pulled it, it stretched and stayed stretched, a tired little bulge. When she pulled again, it tore.
'See,' said her mother. 'When it stops coming back, it is close to breaking.'
Ammu said yes, Amma, the way you say yes to things you are not really listening to. It was August, and Onam was coming, and Onam meant the swing.

Every year the children of the lane hung an oonjal, a festival swing, from the big mango tree at the end of the path. It was a plank seat on two long ropes, decorated with marigolds and mango leaves. This year Biju, who was twelve and the leader of everything, had a plan. 'The low branch is for babies,' he said. 'We'll use the high one. The swing will go up past the roof of the shed.'
The high branch was thinner. It stuck out over the path like an arm reaching for something. Biju climbed up and knotted the ropes round it, and everyone cheered.

On the first day, the swing was glorious. When Biju swung, the branch bent down under him like a fishing rod, and lifted him up again, so that every swing had an extra bounce at the bottom. The children shrieked. They queued all afternoon. Ammu had three turns. At the top of each one she could see over the shed and across the whole green sea of rubber trees, and her stomach floated up into her throat.
On the second day, the bigger boys started swinging two at a time, standing up, pumping as hard as they could. 'Higher!' they yelled. 'Make it fly!'
Ammu was waiting her turn when she noticed something. When the two boys jumped off, the swing hung still. And the branch did not go all the way back up.

She looked again. In the morning, the swing's plank had hung level with her chin. Now it hung level with her shoulder. The branch had bent and stayed bent, just a little, the way the old rubber sheet had stretched and stayed stretched.
She went cold all over, even in the August heat.
'Biju,' she said. 'The branch is tired.'
Biju laughed. Everyone laughed. 'Branches don't get tired,' he said. 'It bounced me all day yesterday.'
'It bounced back yesterday,' said Ammu. 'It isn't bouncing back now. Look at the seat. It's lower.'

'You're scared because you're small,' said one of the boys, and the others made chicken noises. Ammu's face went hot. She wanted to be quiet. Being quiet would have been much easier. But she thought of the old sheet, the tired bulge, and the sound it made when it tore.
Her little sister Kunju was next in the queue, holding up her arms to be lifted on.
'No,' said Ammu, and she pulled Kunju back by her frock, so hard that Kunju began to cry.
'Fine,' said Biju. 'Then I'll show you.' He climbed onto the plank, stood up, and pumped once, twice, three times, swinging higher than the shed roof.
On the fourth swing there was a sound like a coconut splitting.

The branch did not snap all at once. It cracked, and sagged, and Biju, at the bottom of the swing, felt the ropes go soft in his hands. He jumped. He landed on his knees in the mud of the path. A second later the whole branch, ropes, marigolds and all, came down with a heavy, leafy crash exactly where Kunju would have been sitting.
Nobody said anything for a long time. A crow, offended, flew off into the rubber trees.
Biju stood up slowly. His knees were muddy and his face was white. He looked at the broken branch, with its pale, splintered end. Then he looked at Ammu.
'How did you know?' he said.

Ammu told him about the sheet. She showed him how the swing had hung lower and lower. 'When something stops coming back,' she said, 'it's near the end.' She didn't say 'I told you.' She didn't need to.

That evening, Ammu's mother walked down the lane and looked at the branch on the ground. She looked at the high stump, and at the low, thick branch that the swing had always hung from before. She did not scold anyone. She only touched Ammu's head on her way home, very lightly.

The next morning, the children hung the swing again, on the low branch. It was not as exciting. It did not go higher than the shed. But after every turn, Ammu watched the seat as the rider jumped off, and every time, the branch lifted it back up to exactly the height of her chin.
On Onam day, Biju pushed Kunju on the swing himself, gently, for nearly an hour.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a branch, like a rubber band or a spring, is elastic. Pushed a little, it bends and springs all the way back. Pushed past its elastic limit, it bends and stays bent. That small bend that does not come back is the warning. The thing has started to change inside, and it is close to breaking. Ammu spots this because she has seen the same thing in an old rubber sheet. Engineers watch for this sign in bridges, cranes and aeroplane wings.
ask: How did Ammu's mother test a rubber sheet? What did it mean when the sheet stayed stretched?
What did Ammu notice about the swing seat after the big boys jumped off?
Why did the branch break on the second day, but not on the first?
Why was it hard for Ammu to speak up? What helped her?
Have you ever seen something that 'stopped coming back'? A rubber band, a spring or a toy? What happened to it next?
art: Dawn in a Kerala rubber plantation, a woman with a head lamp shaving a spiral cut on a tree, white latex running into a coconut-shell cup.
Brown rubber sheets hanging in the smoke of a shed, and Ammu's mother pulling a corner of one between finger and thumb.
An Onam swing decorated with marigolds hanging from a high, thin mango branch, children queueing below.
Ammu staring at the empty swing seat, which now hangs at her shoulder, the branch bent lower than before.
The branch cracking and falling with its ropes and flowers, Biju landing in the mud, Ammu holding her little sister back.
The swing hung again from the low, thick branch, Ammu watching the seat rise back to the height of her chin.

games.title: Spring Back, Stay or Snap?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out
items: TEST IT: stretch a rubber band a little and let go. What does it do?
TEST IT: squeeze a ball of atta dough. Does it spring back?
TEST IT: bend a plastic ruler a little and let go. Then put it away. Don't bend it till it snaps!
TEST IT: pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: if you stretch, squash or bend this thing, will it spring back, stay changed, or snap? Put the card on that mat.
Then name one place where that thing is useful because it behaves that way. A good idea wins one spring token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor labelled SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP, with a pile of face-down cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats and put the cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says 'Rubber band' over the SPRING BACK mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and put it on a mat.

setup.art: Children doing a TEST IT card, one stretching a rubber band, one pressing dough.
setup.caption: 3. TEST IT cards: everyone tries it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor: SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the spring tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Here are three mats. Spring back, stay changed and snap. Before we start, can you think of one thing for each mat? Why does it belong there?
flow.kid: Put the three mats on the floor. Spring back, stay, and snap. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, pick a mat.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spring Back, Stay or Snap?. It is a card game about which things are elastic. Here you set up the game.

ask.q: Name one thing for each mat, and say why.
good: A hair band springs back, because it goes back to its loop.

flow.do: Find the card 'Pen spring, pulled very hard'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with a tricky one. A pen spring, pulled very hard. Does it spring back, stay, or snap?
flow.kid: Practice card: a pen spring, pulled very hard. Spring back, stay or snap? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why does a spring pulled very hard stay long?
good: It was stretched too far, so it can't come back.

check.q: A pen spring pulled very hard. Which mat does it go on?
check.why: Game moment: STAY is right. Pulled gently, the spring would go on SPRING BACK. Pulled very hard, it passes its elastic limit and stays long. Picking SNAP usually means 'too far' is pictured as always breaking. Springs usually stretch out first.

flow.parent: The same spring pulled gently goes on SPRING BACK. This shows that one thing can be elastic up to a limit, and then stay changed.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They name a place where that behaviour is useful. 3. Give one token for each good idea.
flow.say: Put your card on a mat. Then tell me one place where it helps that this thing springs back, stays or snaps.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Then say where that is useful. Each good idea wins a 🌀 token.
flow.parent: Good ideas: a hair band must spring back, or it would fall off. Playdough must stay, or you could not make shapes. A papad snapping is how you know it is crisp. Some cards are tricky. A sponge springs back. Crumpled foil stays. A spider web springs back, which is how it catches flies without breaking.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll try it and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: You pinched the skin on your hand. Why did it spring back?
good: It has stretchy stuff inside it, called elastin.

flow.think: Can one thing be on two mats? When?

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Then look at the three piles together.
flow.say: Look at the three piles. Which pile is biggest? Which things were the hardest to decide?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now look at the piles. Which things were hard to decide? Why?
flow.think: Steel, glass and stone are a little elastic too. Do you think anything is never elastic at all?

games.context: This is a card game about elastic things. Elastic means a thing springs back to its shape when you let go. For each thing on a card, players decide: does it spring back, stay changed, or snap?

games.title: Human Springs
games.players: 2 to 6 players, with one grown-up as the caller

printables.title: 16 caller cards
items: STIFF SPRING: move only half as far
FLOPPY SPRING: move twice as far
COLD RUBBER: spring back very slowly
TOO FAR! You pass your limit and stay where you are
TOO FAR! You snap and sit down
STORE IT: crouch and hold, then jump on 'Let go!'

rules: Each player is a spring. Stand on a spot marked with a chappal. That is your resting place.
The caller reads a card. For each gentle pull, the spring takes one step forward. For each gentle push, it takes one step back.
On 'Let go!', every spring jumps back to its resting place.
Special cards change the rules for one round, like STIFF SPRING or TOO FAR.
A spring that moves the wrong number of steps sits out one round. Play until every card has been read.

setup.art: Children standing in a line, each beside a chappal on the floor marking their resting place.
setup.caption: 1. Each spring stands by its chappal.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while a child takes two big steps forward.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads a card. Springs move that many steps.

setup.art: The children jumping back to their chappals as the caller shouts 'Let go!'.
setup.caption: 3. On 'Let go!', everyone springs back.

flow.do: 1. Put one chappal on the floor for each player, in a line with space in front. 2. Each player stands beside a chappal. 3. Shuffle the caller cards.
flow.say: You are all springs. Your chappal is where you rest. When I pull, you stretch forward. When I push, you squash back. When I say 'Let go', you spring home.
flow.kid: You are a spring! Stand by your chappal. That is your home. A pull means step forward. Let go means jump home.
flow.context: This is the first step of Human Springs, an acting game. Each player pretends to be a spring that stretches, squashes and springs back. The founder of DeepKids suggested this game.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Check that each spring moves the right number of steps: one pull, one step.
flow.say: Two gentle pulls! Now let go! Did everyone spring all the way home?
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. One pull, one step. Two pulls, two steps. Let go means jump home!

ask.q: Three pulls made you move three steps. What would six pulls do?

flow.parent: This acts out the spring rule: double the pull, double the stretch. Robert Hooke wrote this rule down in 1678.

flow.do: Read the special cards: STIFF SPRING, FLOPPY SPRING, COLD RUBBER, TOO FAR and STORE IT.
flow.say: Too far! You've passed your limit. When I say let go, you can't get home. You stay where you are.
flow.kid: Special card! A stiff spring moves only a little. Too far means you can't get home. Act it out!

check.q: A spring is pulled TOO FAR, past its limit. When you let go, what happens?
options: It springs all the way back
It stays stretched, or it snaps
check.why: Game moment: a spring pulled past its limit cannot get home. It stays stretched or snaps. Picking 'springs all the way back' means elastic was thought to have no limit. Picking 'shorter' mixes up stretching with squashing.

flow.parent: COLD RUBBER links to a true story. Cold rubber springs back slowly. That mattered on the space shuttle Challenger in 1986. Tell it only if your child is ready for a sad story.

flow.do: Finish with STORE IT and BOUNCE. Everyone crouches, holds, then jumps on 'Let go!'.
flow.say: Crouch down and hold it. You are a squashed spring, full of stored energy. Let go!
flow.kid: Crouch low and hold. You are a squashed spring. Wait for it. Let go! Jump!
flow.think: When you crouch before a jump, your legs are like springs. Where in your body are the springs?

games.context: This is an acting game. Each child is a spring. They stretch when the caller pulls, squash when the caller pushes, and spring back home on 'Let go!'.

items.p: What does elastic mean?
opts: It changes shape when pushed or pulled, and springs back when you let go
items.why: Elastic things spring back to their old shape. Picking 'soft' is a common idea, but steel springs are hard and still elastic. Picking 'made of rubber' misses springs, sponges and skin.
items.art: A rubber band stretched and then back to normal.

items.p: Which of these is elastic?
items.why: A hair band springs back. Playdough and wet clay stay changed. A papad snaps. Picking playdough often means 'it changes shape' was mixed up with 'it springs back'. Elastic needs both.

items.p: A thing that springs back after being stretched is called ____.
items.why: Elastic things, like rubber bands, go back to their old shape when you let go.

items.p: Sort these. Do they spring back, stay changed, or snap?
items.why: Sponges and rubber bands are elastic. Playdough and gum keep their new shape. Twigs and glass hardly bend before they break.

items.p: In the coin stretch test, you add more coins to the cup. What happens to the rubber band?
items.why: More coins pull down harder, so the band stretches more. Picking 'shorter' sometimes comes from thinking the band 'fights back' and pulls itself up. It does pull back, but it still gets longer.
items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time.

items.p: Steel is a little bit elastic.
items.why: True. Steel springs back too. It just needs a much bigger force to stretch or bend it. That is why springs are made of steel.

items.p: You can stretch a spring as far as you like, and it will always spring back.
items.why: False. Every spring has an elastic limit. Pull it past that and it stays stretched, or it breaks.

items.p: A pen spring was pulled very hard. Now it stays long and loose. Why?
opts: It went past its elastic limit
items.why: Past the elastic limit, a spring stays stretched. Picking 'never elastic' misses that it did spring back when pulled gently.
items.context: In the Find the Limit experiment, you stretch different things and measure them before and after.

items.p: Match each spring to its job.
items.why: Springs are used wherever something must push or pull back, or soak up a bump.

items.p: You squash the pen spring all the way down and let go. Then you squash it only halfway. Which jumps higher?
items.why: Squashing more stores more energy, so it jumps higher. Picking 'both the same' often means the spring is pictured as having one fixed jump. In fact the jump depends on how much you squash it.
items.context: In the Pen Spring Jump, you squash the small spring from a clicky pen beside a ruler, and let it jump.

items.p: Why does a ball of dough not bounce?
opts: It is not elastic, so it squashes and stays squashed
items.why: A bounce is a squash and a spring back. Dough squashes but does not spring back. Picking 'too heavy' is a common guess. But a heavy rubber ball still bounces.

items.p: A stretched catapult stores ____, which flings the paper ball when you let go.
items.why: Stretching an elastic thing stores energy. Letting go gives it back as movement.

items.p: Which part of your body works like a spring when you jump?
opts: The tendon at the back of your ankle
items.why: Your Achilles tendon stretches as you land and springs back as you push off. Hair is a little stretchy too, but it does not help you jump.

items.p: Name two springs or elastic things in your home. Say what job each one does.
items.a: Any two good examples, each with a job. For example: the spring in my pen pushes the tip back in. The elastic in my socks stops them falling down.
items.why: Any two correct examples, each with a job, are right.

items.p: Draw a rubber band before and after you stretch it. Draw an arrow to show which way it pulls back on your fingers.
items.a: Two drawings: a small loop, then a long loop. The pull-back arrows point inwards, towards the middle of the band.
items.why: A stretched band pulls back towards its old shape. That pull-back force points inwards.
items.art: Two fingers holding a stretched band, with space for arrows.

items.p: Look at the line graph from the coin stretch test. With 0 coins the band was 10 cm. With 10 coins it was 12 cm. How long was it with 20 coins?
items.why: Each 5 coins added 1 cm. 20 coins is 4 lots of 5, so the band grew 4 cm. 10 + 4 = 14 cm. Picking 20 cm usually means the coins were counted as centimetres.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: The line on the coin stretch graph is straight. What does that tell us?
opts: Each 5 coins added the same extra length
items.why: A straight line means the same change each step. This is the spring rule: double the pull, about double the stretch. Picking 'did not stretch' mixes up a flat line with a straight sloping line.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

items.p: A thick rubber band and a thin one hold the same coins. The thick one stretches less. What do scientists call the thick band?
items.why: A stiff spring needs a bigger pull to stretch the same amount. Picking 'weaker' is a common idea. In fact the thick band can usually hold more before it snaps.

items.p: Look at the bounce test chart. Which ball is the most elastic?
items.why: The rubber ball bounced back highest, 80 cm out of 100 cm. It springs back best and loses the least energy. Picking the sponge ball often means soft is thought to be springy. Soft is not the same as elastic.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

items.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high they bounce back.

items.p: A good rubber ball dropped from 1 metre can bounce back higher than 1 metre.
items.why: False. Some energy always turns into heat and sound when it squashes. So it never comes all the way back up, unless someone throws it down.

items.p: Why does a bamboo tree bend in a storm instead of snapping?
opts: It is elastic, so it bends, stores the push, and springs back
items.why: Springy things soak up a sudden push by bending. Picking 'dead inside' is the opposite. Dry, dead wood is the kind that snaps.

items.p: In the story 'The Tired Branch', Ammu saw the swing seat hanging lower after the boys jumped off. What did that tell her?
opts: The branch had passed its elastic limit and might break
The ropes had got longer in the sun
items.why: The branch had bent and stayed bent, so it was no longer springing back. That is the warning sign of the elastic limit. Picking 'the ropes got longer' is a sensible guess, but the branch was what had sagged.
items.context: In this unit's story, children in Kerala hang an Onam swing from a thin, high mango branch and swing on it very hard.

items.p: Ammu's mother pulls the corner of a rubber sheet. An old sheet stretches and stays stretched. What idea does this show?
items.why: A good sheet springs back. An old, sun-damaged sheet stays stretched, because it has passed its limit. Soon it tears. Picking 'friction' mixes up rubbing with stretching.
items.context: In this unit's story, Ammu's mother makes rubber sheets in Kerala. She tests each one by pulling a corner.

items.p: Sort these by what they store energy in.
items.why: A catapult band, a bow string and trampoline springs are stretched. A pen spring and a ball are squashed. The car's band is twisted round the axle.

items.p: The rubber band car went 60 cm with 5 winds and 180 cm with 15 winds. Why?
items.why: Each wind twists the band more and stores more energy. Picking 'lighter' or 'floor changed' means wanting another cause. In a fair test, only the winds changed.
items.context: In the Rubber Band Car project, you twist a rubber band round the back axle by winding the wheels backwards.

items.p: One rubber band stretches 4 cm with 20 coins. Two of the same bands hang side by side, holding the same 20 coins. About how far do they stretch?
items.why: Side by side, each band carries only half the coins, so each stretches about half as far: 2 cm. Picking 8 cm usually means two bands were pictured adding their stretch. That happens only when they are joined in a row.
items.context: In the Two in a Row activity, you hang the same coins from one band, from two bands in a chain, and from two bands side by side.

items.p: Match each living thing to its spring.
items.why: Living things use elastic parts to jump, catch food and stay in one piece.

items.p: Why does your skin spring back after a pinch?
opts: It has a stretchy stuff called elastin
items.why: Elastin is a stretchy material in skin, lungs and blood vessels. Picking 'blood pushes it back' is a sensible guess. But the skin springs back by itself. Old skin has less elastin, so it springs back more slowly. Picking 'rubber' is close in spirit, because elastin is rubbery, but it is made by your body.

items.p: A spring balance at a vegetable shop has a spring inside. Why does a heavier bag of onions move the pointer further?
items.a: A heavier bag pulls down harder on the spring. A bigger pull stretches the spring further, so the pointer moves further down the scale.
items.why: The spring rule: a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch. The unit on measuring forces looks at this more.

items.p: Draw the catapult from the Catapult Challenge. Label where the energy is stored before you let go.
items.a: A drawing of the catapult with the arm pressed down. The label points to the bent arm or the stretched rubber bands.
items.why: The bent stick and stretched bands store the energy. When you let go, they spring back and fling the ball.
items.art: An empty box to draw in.

items.p: Deep down, why does a steel spring spring back?
opts: Its atoms are held by electric pulls that act like tiny springs
It has tiny rubber bands inside
items.why: Bonds between atoms pull them back to their places. Picking 'tiny rubber bands' is a nice picture, but there is no rubber in steel. Picking gravity misses that springs work sideways and upside down too.

items.p: Rubber springs back for a different reason. What is rubber made of?
opts: Long tangled chains, like cooked noodles
Neat rows of atoms, like steel
items.why: Rubber is made of polymers, long tangled chains. Stretching straightens them. Jiggling shakes them back into a tangle. Picking 'neat rows' is how steel is built, not rubber.

items.p: Past the elastic limit, a steel spring stays stretched. What happens to its atoms?
opts: Rows of atoms slip, and each atom settles beside new neighbours
items.why: Below the limit, bonds just stretch and pull back. Past it, rows of atoms slip over each other and rest in new places. Picking 'disappear' is a common guess, but atoms are never lost. They only move.

items.p: A stretched rubber band pulls harder when you warm it.
items.why: True. Warmth makes rubber's chains jiggle more, so they pull back into a tangle harder. This is the opposite of most materials, which get a little longer when warm.

items.p: What causes an earthquake?
opts: Rock slowly bends underground, then suddenly slips and springs back
Heavy buildings press the ground down
items.why: Harry Fielding Reid explained this in 1910. Picking 'heavy buildings' is a common worry, but earthquakes start many kilometres underground, far below any building.
items.context: Rock deep underground is slowly bent as the Earth's giant pieces move.

items.p: In the ruler earthquake, you press a ruler's end down until it slips off your finger. The twang is like…
opts: The shaking when bent rock slips
items.why: The bent ruler stores energy, then lets it all go at once. Bent rock does the same in an earthquake.
items.context: In the Bend or Snap? activity, you hold a ruler on a table and slowly press its free end down until it slips.

items.p: In 2015, LIGO caught a gravitational wave. What did the wave do to LIGO's 4-kilometre arms?
opts: Stretched and squeezed them by far less than the width of an atom
items.why: The stretch was less than a hundredth of the width of a proton. A proton is a tiny speck inside an atom. Picking '1 metre' shows how hard it is to imagine something so small. That is why LIGO took decades to build.
items.context: A gravitational wave is a ripple in space itself. It stretches space one way and squeezes it the other way.

items.p: In Rubber Band Galaxies, you stretched a strip with dots on it. Which dot moved furthest from dot A?
items.why: When the whole strip stretches, far dots move away faster. Astronomers see the same with galaxies. Picking 'all the same' misses that each piece of rubber between dots stretches, so more rubber means more stretch.

items.p: Scientists know exactly what space is made of.
items.why: False. We have measured space stretching, but nobody knows what space is made of. String theory and loop quantum gravity are ideas with no evidence yet.

items.p: Who made bouncy rubber balls about 3,500 years ago?
opts: People in ancient Mexico and Central America
items.why: Dorothy Hosler's team showed in 1999 how they mixed rubber-tree sap with morning glory juice. Picking Goodyear is common, because books credit him. He lived about 3,400 years later.

items.p: Why did the cold matter for the rubber seals on the space shuttle Challenger?
opts: Cold rubber springs back too slowly to seal the gap
items.why: Cold rubber goes stiff, so it springs back slowly. The engineer Roger Boisjoly warned about this. Picking 'melts' mixes up cold with heat.
items.context: In January 1986, the space shuttle Challenger launched on a freezing morning. Rubber rings sealed the joints in its rockets.

items.p: Robert Hooke hid his spring rule in a code of jumbled letters in 1676. Why might he have done this?
opts: So nobody could claim it before he was ready to explain it
items.why: Scientists sometimes did this to prove later that they had the idea first. Picking 'a joke' is a fair guess for something so odd. But it was a serious way to protect his claim.

items.p: Spider silk is very stretchy, and weight for weight stronger than steel wire. Does that change the idea that stretchy things are weak? Explain.
items.a: Yes. Spider silk shows that a thing can be both stretchy and strong. Stretching lets it soak up a fly hitting the web without snapping.
items.why: Being able to stretch can make a material tougher, because it soaks up sudden pushes.

items.p: In the bungee doll challenge, 2 bands let the doll fall 30 cm, 3 bands 40 cm and 4 bands 50 cm. Describe the pattern. Then predict 8 bands.
items.a: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 4 bands is 50 cm, so 8 bands is 4 more bands, which is 40 cm more. 50 + 40 = 90 cm.
items.why: The pattern goes up by the same amount each time, like the spring rule. Real rubber bands may curve a little near their limit.

items.p: Is it better to be stiff or to bend? Give one example where stiff is better and one where bending is better.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: a ruler for drawing lines should be stiff. A bridge in a storm, or a tree, is better if it can bend and spring back.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a good example for each side.

items.p: Draw a model of atoms in a spring, as balls joined by tiny springs. Draw it again when the spring is stretched.
items.a: Two drawings. In the first, balls are evenly spaced with short springs between them. In the second, the balls are a little further apart and the springs are longer.
items.why: Stretching a spring stretches the bonds between its atoms a tiny bit each.

items.p: Robert Hooke used a wire 20 to 40 feet long, about 6 to 12 metres, to measure stretch. Why does a long wire help?
items.a: A long wire has many more bits, or bonds, in a row. Each bit stretches a tiny amount, and all the tiny amounts add up to a stretch big enough to measure.
items.why: This is the same reason two bands in a chain stretch twice as far as one.

experiments.title: Coin by Coin: find the pattern, find the limit
experiments.context: This is the coin test. You hang a cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time, measuring the band each time. Then you pull a pen spring a little further each time, to find where it stops coming back.
experiments.question: When you add coins in equal handfuls, how does a rubber band's length change? And how far can a spring be pulled before it stops coming back?
experiments.predict: Before you add any coins, guess. Each time we add 5 coins, will the band grow by the same amount? By more and more? Or by less and less? Why do you think so? And if we pull a spring further and further, will it always come back? Why?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of coins. Use the same band, the same cup, the same kind of coins and the same ruler. Add exactly 5 coins each time. Wait until the cup stops bouncing, and read the ruler at eye level at the bottom of the band. For the pen spring, change only how far you pull it.

materials.item: a thin rubber band, the ordinary kind used to close a packet
a small paper cup, with a string handle threaded through two holes near the rim
40 coins of the same kind, such as 1-rupee coins. If you have fewer, use 8 AA batteries of the same kind and add one at a time
a pencil, and two chairs to rest it on
a 30 cm ruler and some tape
the spring from an old clicky ballpoint pen

experiments.safety: Stand to the side, not over the cup, in case the band slips. A grown-up takes the spring out of the pen. Keep the spring's ends away from eyes.

schedule.what: Guess with a reason, add coins 5 at a time and measure, then pull a pen spring further each time until it stops coming back.

experiments.record: Fill in the coin table. Then make a second table for the pen spring. One column says how far you pulled it. The other says its length after you let go. Circle the first pull it did not come back from.
